meta.scope: Corporate IT, Microsoft 365 and the three site networks. Excludes plant OT/SCADA and the cold chain telemetry platform.
meta.framework: NIST CSF 2.0 with CIS Controls v8.1

GV.OC-01.pn: Mission and objectives are stated in the group business plan; the IT/security policy references it in the introduction but does not translate it into risk priorities.
GV.OC-01.in: Security work is driven by audit findings and customer questionnaires rather than by mission impact. No documented link from production continuity to control selection.

GV.OC-02.pn: Stakeholder expectations captured only where a customer contract demands it (two retail accounts have security schedules).
GV.OC-02.in: No stakeholder register. Retail customer security requirements are handled ad hoc by the account team and not routed to IT.

GV.OC-03.pn: Legal and regulatory register maintained by the compliance manager; covers GDPR, food safety and, since March, NIS2 as an important entity.
GV.OC-03.in: GDPR obligations are operationalised (DPIA process, ROPA). NIS2 obligations identified in a gap paper but not yet assigned owners or dates.

GV.OC-04.pn: Business impact analysis completed in 2024 identifies order-to-dispatch, cold chain telemetry and payroll as critical.
GV.OC-04.in: BIA outputs feed the DR plan but have not been revisited since the Little Island site was integrated. Cold chain telemetry is out of this assessment's scope.

GV.OC-05.pn: Dependency list exists for IT services (M365, Azure, the ERP host and the EDI broker) inside the DR plan.
GV.OC-05.in: Dependencies are known to the IT team but not mapped to business functions, and single points of failure are not tracked anywhere formal.

GV.RM-01.pn: No documented risk management objectives. Security objectives appear only as line items in the annual IT plan.
GV.RM-01.in: Objectives are effectively 'pass the customer audits'. Nothing measurable is agreed with the board.

GV.RM-02.pn: No risk appetite or tolerance statement exists at any level.
GV.RM-02.in: Risk acceptance happens verbally in the IT steering meeting with no threshold, no record and no expiry.
GV.RM-02.rec: Draft a one-page risk appetite statement for approval by the Operations Director at the next IT steering meeting, expressed in terms the business already uses (production downtime hours, order-to-dispatch disruption, personal data exposure). This unblocks GV.RM-04 and gives the steering committee a basis for recording risk acceptance with an expiry date.

GV.RM-03.pn: Enterprise risk register is maintained by finance and contains one line for 'IT/cyber'.
GV.RM-03.in: Cyber risks are not aggregated with enterprise risk. The single register entry has not been updated in 14 months.

GV.RM-04.pn: No documented risk response options. Cyber insurance was renewed in January without a documented risk basis.
GV.RM-04.in: Response decisions are made case by case by the IT manager. Shared-responsibility boundaries for Azure and the ERP host are undocumented.

GV.RM-05.pn: IT steering committee terms of reference name security as a standing agenda item.
GV.RM-05.in: Steering meets monthly and security is discussed, but there is no upward escalation path to the board and no route for suppliers to raise risk.

GV.RM-06.pn: No standardised risk calculation method. The one register entry uses an unlabelled high/medium/low.
GV.RM-06.in: Qualys TruRisk scoring is used for vulnerabilities, which is consistent, but nothing equivalent exists for non-technical risk.

GV.RM-07.pn: Positive risk / opportunity is not addressed in any documentation.
GV.RM-07.in: Not performed. Noted as low priority relative to the other Govern gaps.

GV.RR-01.pn: The Operations Director is named as the accountable executive in the information security policy.
GV.RR-01.in: Leadership engages when customers or auditors ask, and funded the Sophos and Qualys renewals without challenge, but does not set direction or review outcomes.

GV.RR-02.pn: Policy names an IT Manager, a part-time security lead and a compliance manager. No RACI for security activities.
GV.RR-02.in: Roles are understood inside IT. Outside IT, staff do not know who owns security decisions; three interviewees named the wrong person.

GV.RR-03.pn: No documented resourcing model. Headcount is agreed annually with no reference to the risk strategy.
GV.RR-03.in: Security is approximately 0.4 FTE of the IT Manager's time plus the MSP retainer. Vulnerability remediation is visibly resource-constrained.

GV.RR-04.pn: HR policy covers pre-employment screening, the acceptable use policy in the contract of employment, and a documented leavers process.
GV.RR-04.in: Screening and AUP signature are consistently evidenced. Leaver deprovisioning is triggered from the HR system, though the sample showed two accounts disabled 4 and 9 days late.

GV.PO-01.pn: Information security policy plus eight supporting policies, approved by the Operations Director in 2023. Scope, roles and enforcement statements are all present.
GV.PO-01.in: Policies are published on the intranet and referenced in induction. Content is not consistently reflected in practice — the remote access policy still describes the retired SSL VPN.

GV.PO-02.pn: Policy states an annual review cycle.
GV.PO-02.in: Last full review was 22 months ago. No evidence of communication of changes, and no enforcement or exception mechanism.

GV.OV-01.pn: No documented review of strategy outcomes.
GV.OV-01.in: The IT plan is refreshed annually but is not informed by any measurement of whether prior security work reduced risk.

GV.OV-02.pn: No process for reviewing whether the strategy still covers organisational requirements.
GV.OV-02.in: The Little Island acquisition (2025) has not triggered any reassessment of the security approach.

GV.OV-03.pn: No defined security KPIs or metrics.
GV.OV-03.in: Patch compliance and phishing simulation rates are visible in Sophos and M365 but are not reported, trended or acted on as performance measures.

GV.SC-01.pn: No supply chain risk management programme, strategy or policy. The procurement policy is silent on cybersecurity.
GV.SC-01.in: Not performed. This is the single largest gap in the assessment and is directly relevant to NIS2 Article 21(2)(d).
GV.SC-01.rec: Stand up a supplier assurance programme owned jointly by the compliance manager and procurement, starting with the 11 material IT suppliers already identified during this assessment. Minimum viable version: a one-page security schedule for contracts, a tiered questionnaire, and an annual reassessment date for the four Tier 1 suppliers. This is the single largest NIS2 exposure and should be started before the next audit cycle.

GV.SC-02.pn: Security responsibilities appear in two of the eleven material supplier contracts reviewed, both driven by the supplier's own paper.
GV.SC-02.in: No standard security schedule. The ERP hosting contract has no security obligations at all.

GV.SC-03.pn: Supply chain risk is not integrated into any risk management process.

GV.SC-04.pn: Finance maintains an approved supplier list with spend-based tiering.
GV.SC-04.in: The list is accurate for spend but does not identify which suppliers touch data or systems. IT built an informal list of 11 material IT suppliers for this assessment.

GV.SC-05.pn: No standard security requirements exist for inclusion in contracts or tenders.
GV.SC-05.in: Requirements are only raised when a customer flows them down to Kilcarn first.

GV.SC-06.pn: No due diligence procedure before onboarding a supplier.
GV.SC-06.in: The most recent IT supplier (the EDI broker) was onboarded in April with no security review; the assessor could not locate a SOC 2 report or equivalent.

GV.SC-07.pn: No documented approach to understanding or monitoring third-party risk over the relationship.
GV.SC-07.in: No supplier reassessment, no monitoring of supplier security notices. The 2025 EDI broker outage was handled as an availability issue only.

GV.SC-08.pn: The incident response plan does not reference suppliers or define their role.
GV.SC-08.in: Not performed. The MSP has no contractual incident obligations and no agreed contact path outside the service desk.

GV.SC-09.pn: Supply chain practices are not integrated into product or service lifecycle management.

GV.SC-10.pn: No offboarding provisions for suppliers in policy or contract.
GV.SC-10.in: Data return and account termination are handled informally. Two dormant accounts belonging to a supplier disengaged in 2024 were still enabled at the time of testing.

ID.AM-01.pn: Asset management procedure defines ownership, tagging and a quarterly reconciliation.
ID.AM-01.in: Intune and vSphere give good coverage of laptops and VMs. Reconciliation is not actually quarterly, and 34 network devices and the Little Island server room are tracked only in a spreadsheet.

ID.AM-02.pn: Software asset procedure covers approval, licensing and removal.
ID.AM-02.in: Intune discovery and Sophos give a reliable list for managed endpoints. Server-side software is not inventoried centrally; two out-of-support applications were found on the ERP host.

ID.AM-03.pn: Network documentation standard exists as part of the change process.
ID.AM-03.in: Core diagrams exist and are broadly accurate for HQ. Little Island was integrated in 2025 and the diagram has not been updated. No data-flow diagrams.

ID.AM-04.pn: No requirement to inventory supplier-provided services.
ID.AM-04.in: The 11-supplier list built for this assessment is the only artefact. Shadow SaaS is not discovered.

ID.AM-05.pn: Criticality tiers defined in the BIA (Tier 1 to Tier 3).
ID.AM-05.in: Tiering is applied to the eight named business systems but not to the underlying assets, so patch and backup priority is not driven by criticality.

ID.AM-07.pn: Data inventory is required by the GDPR policy.
ID.AM-07.in: The ROPA covers personal data reasonably well. Commercially sensitive data (recipes, pricing, retail forecasts) is not inventoried or classified at all.

ID.AM-08.pn: Lifecycle is covered for endpoints in the asset procedure; nothing equivalent for servers, network or SaaS.
ID.AM-08.in: Endpoint refresh runs on a four-year cycle with certified disposal. Server and appliance end-of-life is reactive — two switches are past vendor end-of-support.

ID.RA-01.pn: Vulnerability management procedure defines scan cadence, TruRisk-based prioritisation and remediation SLAs by severity.
ID.RA-01.in: Qualys VMDR runs authenticated scans weekly across servers and endpoints and daily on the external perimeter. Findings are tracked to closure in the IT ticket queue. Strongest control in the assessment.

ID.RA-02.in: The IT Manager subscribes to NCSC-IE and Sophos advisories and acts on them. Consumption is personal rather than institutional and stops when he is on leave.

ID.RA-03.in: Threats are not recorded anywhere. No threat modelling for the ERP or EDI integration.

ID.RA-04.pn: No impact and likelihood methodology outside the vulnerability process.
ID.RA-04.in: TruRisk covers technical exposure well; business impact of non-technical threats is not assessed.

ID.RA-05.in: Prioritisation is effectively CVSS/TruRisk driven, which under-weights process and supplier risk.

ID.RA-06.pn: Remediation SLAs are documented for vulnerabilities only.
ID.RA-06.in: Vulnerability responses are tracked well. Risk responses arising from audits or incidents are captured in meeting minutes and frequently lost.

ID.RA-07.pn: Change management procedure requires a risk statement, approval and rollback plan for standard and major changes.
ID.RA-07.in: CAB meets weekly and records are complete for infrastructure change. Emergency changes are retrospectively documented; three of eight sampled were missing the risk assessment. Exceptions have no expiry date.

ID.RA-08.pn: No vulnerability disclosure policy and no published contact.
ID.RA-08.in: Not performed. security@ alias does not exist; a 2025 researcher report reached the general info@ mailbox and sat for 11 days.

ID.RA-09.pn: No requirement to verify authenticity or integrity of hardware and software before use.
ID.RA-09.in: Software is generally acquired from vendor portals and Microsoft Store, so practice is reasonable, but hash or signature verification is not performed or evidenced.

ID.RA-10.pn: No pre-acquisition assessment requirement for critical suppliers.

ID.IM-01.pn: Audit and assessment findings are expected to be actioned; no documented improvement process.
ID.IM-01.in: Findings from the 2025 retail customer audit were tracked in a spreadsheet to closure, which shows the capability exists. It is not repeatable or owned.

ID.IM-02.pn: Testing is required annually by policy (penetration test only).
ID.IM-02.in: External penetration test performed in November 2025; six of the fourteen findings remain open with no dates. No exercises of any kind.

ID.IM-03.pn: No process for capturing improvements from day-to-day operations.
ID.IM-03.in: Good ideas surface in the weekly IT meeting and are not recorded.

ID.IM-04.pn: Incident response plan and DR plan both exist and were approved in 2025.
ID.IM-04.in: Plans are documented and stored on SharePoint and in the offline runbook copy. Neither has been exercised, and contact lists still name two leavers.

PR.AA-01.pn: Identity and access management policy covers user, admin and service account lifecycle, with a documented JML process.
PR.AA-01.in: Entra ID is authoritative and joiner/leaver is HR-triggered and reliable. Service accounts are the weak point: 23 identified, 9 with no named owner and 4 with non-expiring passwords.

PR.AA-02.pn: Identity proofing requirements are set out in the HR onboarding standard.
PR.AA-02.in: In-person identity verification at induction for site staff, and manager confirmation for remote hires. Contractors follow the same process.

PR.AA-03.pn: Authentication standard requires MFA for all cloud, remote and administrative access, and prohibits shared accounts.
PR.AA-03.in: Entra Conditional Access enforces MFA for all users with no legacy authentication exceptions remaining. Device compliance is required for M365 access. Sampling found no shared interactive accounts.

PR.AA-04.pn: SSO and federation requirements documented for new applications.
PR.AA-04.in: SAML/OIDC SSO in place for eight of eleven business applications. The ERP and two smaller tools still hold local credentials.

PR.AA-05.pn: Access control policy defines least privilege, role-based access and six-monthly recertification.
PR.AA-05.in: RBAC is well implemented in Entra and file services. Recertification has not run since early 2025; the ERP finance role sample showed three users retaining access after moving department.

PR.AA-06.pn: Physical security procedure covers badge issue, visitor escort and server room access.
PR.AA-06.in: Badge access with individual credentials at all three sites, server rooms on a separate access group. Access list review is annual and was completed; visitor log at Ashbourne is inconsistently completed.

PR.AT-01.pn: Awareness policy requires induction training and annual refresher for all staff.
PR.AT-01.in: KnowBe4-style annual module plus monthly phishing simulation. Completion is 94% and the click rate has fallen from 18% to 6% over twelve months.

PR.AT-02.pn: Role-based training is mentioned in policy but not defined for any specific role.
PR.AT-02.in: IT staff receive vendor training on Sophos and vSphere. No security-specific training for privileged users, developers (none in house) or the executive team.

PR.DS-01.pn: Encryption standard requires full-disk encryption on endpoints and encryption at rest for cloud data.
PR.DS-01.in: BitLocker enforced via Intune with keys escrowed in Entra, 100% compliant on managed devices. SQL TDE is not enabled on the ERP database, which holds pricing and customer data.

PR.DS-02.pn: Standard requires TLS 1.2 or better for all data in transit and prohibits plaintext protocols.
PR.DS-02.in: External services are TLS 1.2+ and verified in the last external scan. Internal LDAP signing is enforced; one legacy line-of-business web app on the Ashbourne VLAN is still HTTP only.

PR.DS-10.pn: Data-in-use protection is not addressed in policy.
PR.DS-10.in: No memory protection, enclave or equivalent controls, and none required for this environment. Recorded as a documentation gap rather than a technical one.

PR.DS-11.pn: Backup standard defines 3-2-1, retention of 35 days operational and 12 months archive, and quarterly restore testing.
PR.DS-11.in: Veeam with immutable repository and offsite copy; jobs are monitored and success rate over the period was 99.4%. Restore testing is file-level only and the last full system restore test was 14 months ago.
PR.DS-11.rec: Reinstate the quarterly restore test and extend it to at least one full system recovery per year — the ERP host is the obvious candidate given its Tier 1 status. Schedule the first full test alongside the Q3 tabletop so the recovery capability and the response plan are validated together.

PR.PS-01.pn: Configuration standards documented for Windows 11, Windows Server 2022 and M365, based on CIS Benchmarks Level 1.
PR.PS-01.in: Intune configuration profiles and GPO deliver the baseline for endpoints and domain servers. Drift is not monitored, and the Little Island file server was built manually outside the baseline.

PR.PS-02.pn: Patch policy sets 14 days for critical, 30 for high, 90 for medium, and requires removal of unsupported software.
PR.PS-02.in: Intune and WSUS deliver OS and Microsoft patching reliably (96% within SLA). Third-party patching is manual and lags — Qualys shows 41 endpoints with out-of-date Chrome or Adobe Reader past SLA.

PR.PS-03.pn: Hardware maintenance and disposal covered in the asset procedure with certified destruction.
PR.PS-03.in: Endpoint disposal is evidenced with certificates. Network and server hardware maintenance is reactive; two access switches and the Ashbourne UPS are past end-of-support.

PR.PS-04.pn: Logging standard defines which events must be generated and a 12-month retention requirement.
PR.PS-04.in: Logs are generated on servers, endpoints, firewalls and M365. Retention is met for M365 (Purview) but firewall logs roll at 30 days and vSphere logs at 14, both short of the standard.

PR.PS-05.pn: Policy prohibits unauthorised software and requires application control.
PR.PS-05.in: Users are non-admin on all managed endpoints and Sophos application control blocks known unwanted applications. Full allowlisting (WDAC/AppLocker) is not deployed, so unsigned binaries in user-writable paths can still execute.

PR.PS-06.in: No in-house software development. Two Power Apps and roughly 40 Power Automate flows are built by the finance team with no review, which is where this gap actually bites.

PR.IR-01.pn: Network security standard covers segmentation, firewall change control and remote access.
PR.IR-01.in: Sophos XGS firewalls at each site with a documented ruleset, corporate/guest/OT VLAN separation and Entra-authenticated always-on VPN. East-west traffic within the corporate VLAN is unrestricted.

PR.IR-02.pn: Environmental requirements documented for the HQ and Ashbourne server rooms.
PR.IR-02.in: UPS, HVAC and water detection in place at HQ with monitoring; Ashbourne has UPS and HVAC but no environmental alerting and the UPS is past end-of-support.

PR.IR-03.pn: Resilience requirements documented in the DR plan with RTO 8 hours and RPO 4 hours for Tier 1 systems.
PR.IR-03.in: vSphere HA and replication to Ashbourne provide the technical capability. Failover has never been tested end-to-end, so the stated RTO is unproven.

PR.IR-04.pn: Capacity management is part of the infrastructure standard with defined thresholds.
PR.IR-04.in: PRTG monitors storage, compute and bandwidth with alerting at 80%. Capacity is reviewed monthly and forecasting is documented for the next 12 months.

DE.CM-01.pn: Monitoring standard states that network activity will be monitored; no defined use cases or thresholds.
DE.CM-01.in: Sophos XGS produces IPS and web filtering alerts to the IT mailbox. No netflow collection, no baseline of normal traffic and nothing reviewed out of hours.

DE.CM-02.pn: Physical monitoring requirements documented in the site security procedure.
DE.CM-02.in: CCTV with 31-day retention and door-forced alarms at all three sites, monitored by the facilities provider. Alerts do not reach IT.

DE.CM-03.pn: Acceptable use policy reserves the right to monitor; no procedure defines what is monitored or by whom.
DE.CM-03.in: Entra sign-in risk and impossible-travel alerts are enabled and do fire, but nobody is assigned to review them. 62 risky sign-in alerts were unreviewed at the time of testing.

DE.CM-06.pn: No requirement to monitor external service provider activity.
DE.CM-06.in: The MSP holds Global Administrator and privileged vSphere access. Their activity is not logged to a Kilcarn-controlled destination or reviewed.

DE.CM-09.pn: Endpoint and server monitoring covered in the monitoring standard.
DE.CM-09.in: Sophos Central EDR is deployed on 98% of managed endpoints and all servers, with detections visible in the console. Triage happens in business hours only, and the mean time to acknowledge over the period was 19 hours.

DE.AE-02.pn: Analysis expectations are stated in the incident response plan at a high level.
DE.AE-02.in: Analysis is performed competently by the IT Manager when he picks something up. No playbooks, so quality depends entirely on who is on shift.

DE.AE-03.pn: No requirement to correlate information across sources.
DE.AE-03.in: No SIEM. Firewall, endpoint, identity and M365 signals live in four separate consoles and are only joined manually during an incident.

DE.AE-04.pn: Impact and scope estimation is referenced in the incident response plan.
DE.AE-04.in: Done informally and reasonably well for the two incidents reviewed, but not recorded in a consistent form.

DE.AE-06.pn: Plan states that IT and the Operations Director are informed of significant events.
DE.AE-06.in: Alerts reach a shared IT mailbox. There is no on-call rota, so anything raised after 17:30 on Friday is seen Monday morning.

DE.AE-07.pn: No requirement to integrate threat intelligence into analysis.
DE.AE-07.in: Sophos threat feeds are applied automatically by the product. No manual enrichment, no IOC sweeps against historical data.

DE.AE-08.pn: Incident declaration criteria are defined in the incident response plan with three severity levels.
DE.AE-08.in: The criteria are sensible and written down, but declaration in practice is a judgement call by whoever is available and has not been consistently applied.

RS.MA-01.pn: Incident response plan approved March 2025, defines activation, roles and the response lifecycle.
RS.MA-01.in: The plan was followed for the June 2025 business email compromise and worked. Third parties are not part of it — the MSP and insurer were engaged ad hoc, and the plan has never been exercised.

RS.MA-02.pn: Triage responsibilities are assigned in the plan to the IT Manager or deputy.
RS.MA-02.in: Triage happens through the service desk queue and is generally sound in hours. No documented triage criteria and no out-of-hours capability.

RS.MA-03.pn: Severity matrix in the plan defines P1 to P3 with response and update targets.
RS.MA-03.in: The matrix is clear. Of the seven security tickets sampled, four had no severity recorded at all.

RS.MA-04.pn: Escalation path documented to the Operations Director and, for P1, the managing director.
RS.MA-04.in: The path is understood by IT staff. The 2025 BEC incident reached the Operations Director six hours after detection against a two-hour target.

RS.MA-05.pn: Recovery initiation criteria are stated briefly in the plan.
RS.MA-05.in: Criteria are vague ('once the threat is contained') and there is no documented sign-off step, so the decision to restore is effectively made by whoever is in the room.

RS.AN-03.pn: Root cause analysis is required by the plan for P1 and P2 incidents.
RS.AN-03.in: A root cause was established for the BEC (a legacy authentication path, since closed). No RCA exists for the two P2 incidents in the period.

RS.AN-06.pn: No requirement to record investigative actions or preserve their integrity.
RS.AN-06.in: Investigation notes live in ticket comments and in the IT Manager's OneNote. No timestamped action log, no integrity protection.

RS.AN-07.pn: No evidence handling or chain of custody procedure.
RS.AN-07.in: Evidence collection is ad hoc. During the BEC, mailbox audit logs were exported to a personal OneDrive folder with no hashing.

RS.AN-08.pn: Magnitude estimation is mentioned in the plan.
RS.AN-08.in: Estimated during the BEC (14 mailboxes assessed, 2 confirmed accessed) and reported to the DPO, which was appropriate. Not a repeatable method.

RS.CO-02.pn: Notification requirements documented, including the 72-hour GDPR clock and the NIS2 24-hour early warning.
RS.CO-02.in: The DPO route works and was used correctly in 2025. NIS2 notification steps are written down but no one has walked through them, and the NCSC-IE contact details in the plan are out of date.

RS.CO-03.pn: Information sharing expectations are stated in the plan.
RS.CO-03.in: Internal sharing worked during the BEC. No mechanism for sharing with customers, suppliers or sector peers, and no supplier contact tree.

RS.MI-01.pn: Containment actions are described in the plan by incident type.
RS.MI-01.in: Sophos Central isolation and Entra session revocation are available and were both used effectively in the 2025 incident. Containment is a genuine strength.

RS.MI-02.pn: Eradication steps described in the plan at a general level.
RS.MI-02.in: Eradication relies on rebuild-from-image for endpoints, which is effective. No documented verification step to confirm the threat is gone before returning a system to service.

RC.RP-01.pn: DR plan documents recovery execution with RTO 8 hours and RPO 4 hours for Tier 1.
RC.RP-01.in: The plan is detailed and the Veeam capability is real. Full execution has never been rehearsed, so the RTO remains an assumption.

RC.RP-02.pn: Recovery prioritisation is documented and follows the BIA tiering.
RC.RP-02.in: Prioritisation is sound on paper. Little Island systems were never added after the 2025 integration and do not appear in the recovery order.

RC.RP-03.pn: Standard requires backup integrity verification before any restore.
RC.RP-03.in: Veeam SureBackup verification runs nightly against the immutable repository and results are checked. Integrity of the offsite copy is verified monthly rather than per restore.

RC.RP-04.pn: The plan states that critical functions are considered when setting recovery targets.
RC.RP-04.in: Targets come from the 2024 BIA and are reasonable, but there is no post-incident reassessment step to adjust them.

RC.RP-05.pn: Verification of restored assets is required before return to service.
RC.RP-05.in: File-level restores are verified by the requesting user. There is no technical integrity check on restored systems and no formal return-to-service sign-off.

RC.RP-06.pn: The plan defines who declares the end of an incident.
RC.RP-06.in: Declared verbally for the 2025 incident. Documentation was completed after the fact and the lessons-learned section was left blank.

RC.CO-03.pn: Internal recovery communication is covered in the DR plan with a defined update cadence.
RC.CO-03.in: Communication during the 2025 incident was effective by email and Teams. The cadence in the plan (hourly for P1) was not met, and the plan's contact list names two leavers.

RC.CO-04.pn: The plan says public communication is owned by the managing director with marketing support.
RC.CO-04.in: No holding statements, no approved channels and no rehearsal. If an incident became public, the response would be improvised.

CIS:1.3.pn: Discovery is not required by the asset procedure.
CIS:1.3.in: No active discovery tool. Asset data comes from Intune and vSphere only, so unmanaged devices on the corporate VLAN are invisible.

CIS:1.4.in: DHCP logging is enabled on the Windows DHCP servers but is not used to update the inventory.

CIS:2.4.in: Intune and Sophos provide automated software inventory for endpoints; servers are excluded.

CIS:2.6.pn: Library allowlisting is not addressed in the configuration standard.

CIS:2.7.in: Script allowlisting not implemented. PowerShell Constrained Language Mode is not enforced.

CIS:3.3.pn: Access control expectations are set in the data policy but no classification scheme underpins them.
CIS:3.3.in: NTFS and SharePoint permissions are role-based and reasonably tight; the 2025 review removed 40 stale group memberships. Nothing is driven by data sensitivity because nothing is classified.

CIS:3.4.pn: Retention schedule exists for personal data and finance records.
CIS:3.4.in: Retention is enforced for the ERP and payroll. M365 retention labels are configured but not applied — mailboxes and Teams data are effectively kept indefinitely.

CIS:3.6.in: BitLocker enforced by Intune on all managed endpoints, keys escrowed in Entra, 100% compliance in the last report.

CIS:3.9.in: Sophos device control blocks unencrypted USB write on endpoints. Not enforced on the three shared production-office PCs at Ashbourne.

CIS:3.13.pn: DLP is not required by policy.
CIS:3.13.in: Purview DLP is licensed under E3 for limited scenarios but no policies are configured.

CIS:3.14.in: Sensitive data access is not logged distinctly from general file access.

CIS:4.3.in: 15-minute lock enforced via Intune and GPO across endpoints and servers; verified on sample.

CIS:4.4.in: Windows Firewall enabled on all servers with managed rules via GPO.

CIS:4.5.in: Windows Firewall enforced and locked by Intune profile on all endpoints.

CIS:4.6.pn: Secure management requirements documented in the infrastructure standard.
CIS:4.6.in: Management of servers and M365 is via authenticated, encrypted channels. Two switches are still managed over HTTP on the management VLAN.

CIS:4.7.in: Default accounts renamed or disabled on Windows builds. Default SNMP community strings were found on two older switches.

CIS:4.8.in: Role-based Windows Server installs keep services minimal. No periodic review, and the ERP host runs an unused IIS instance.

CIS:4.9.in: DNS is forced to the internal resolvers and then to a filtered upstream; external DNS is blocked at the firewall.

CIS:4.11.in: Intune remote wipe is available and tested for all corporate laptops and enrolled mobiles.

CIS:4.12.in: Intune app protection policies applied to Outlook and Teams on BYOD, but no full containerisation.

CIS:5.2.pn: Password standard aligns to NCSC guidance with a 14-character minimum and no forced rotation.
CIS:5.2.in: Entra password protection with a custom banned-list is enabled. Local administrator passwords are unique via LAPS on endpoints but not on servers.

CIS:5.3.in: Reviewed manually rather than automatically. The sample found 11 accounts inactive for more than 90 days still enabled, including two supplier accounts.

CIS:5.4.pn: Separate administrative accounts are mandated by the IAM policy.
CIS:5.4.in: Admins hold distinct -adm accounts with no mailbox and no internet browsing; day-to-day accounts have no privilege. Well implemented.

CIS:5.5.pn: Service account register is required by the IAM policy.
CIS:5.5.in: 23 service accounts identified during this assessment; 9 have no named owner and 4 have non-expiring passwords. The register does not exist in practice.

CIS:6.3.in: All internet-facing applications are behind Entra with Conditional Access MFA. No exceptions found.

CIS:6.4.in: Always-on VPN requires Entra MFA plus a compliant device.

CIS:6.5.in: MFA enforced on all administrative roles; PIM is not licensed but standing admin count is low (5).

CIS:6.6.in: No formal inventory of authentication systems. Entra, the ERP local directory and two SaaS local directories are known but undocumented.

CIS:6.7.in: Entra ID is the central access control point for 8 of 11 business applications.

CIS:7.3.in: Intune update rings and WSUS deliver OS patching; 96% within the 14-day critical SLA.

CIS:7.4.in: Microsoft applications patch automatically. Third-party application patching is manual — 41 endpoints past SLA for Chrome or Adobe Reader.

CIS:7.5.in: Qualys authenticated internal scans run weekly across servers and endpoints.

CIS:7.6.in: External perimeter scanned daily by Qualys; results reviewed at the weekly IT meeting.

CIS:7.7.in: Remediation is tracked to closure. Median time to close criticals over the period was 11 days, within the 14-day SLA.

CIS:8.1.pn: 12-month retention required by the logging standard.
CIS:8.1.in: Met for M365 via Purview. Firewall logs roll at 30 days and vSphere at 14, so the standard is not met for two of the four main sources.

CIS:8.3.in: Storage is adequate for current short retention but would not support the 12-month standard without additional capacity.

CIS:8.4.in: NTP is centralised on the domain controllers and synchronised to an external stratum-2 source; verified on sample.

CIS:8.5.in: Default Windows audit policy plus M365 unified audit log. Detailed logging (process creation, PowerShell) is not enabled.

CIS:8.6.in: DNS queries are logged at the resolver but retained for 7 days and never reviewed.

CIS:8.7.in: URL requests are logged by the Sophos web filter with 30-day retention.

CIS:8.8.in: Command-line process auditing is not enabled. This was a material obstacle during the 2025 BEC investigation.

CIS:8.9.pn: Centralisation is stated as an objective in the logging standard.
CIS:8.9.in: No SIEM or central log store. Four separate consoles. This is the root cause of most Detect findings and is the top recommendation from this assessment.
CIS:8.9.rec: Procure and deploy Microsoft Sentinel against the existing E3 tenant, ingesting Entra ID sign-in and audit logs, Defender/Sophos endpoint detections, Sophos XGS firewall syslog and vSphere events. Kilcarn already holds the licence entitlement, so this is a deployment and tuning exercise rather than a new purchase. Sequence this before any further Detect work — it unblocks DE.AE-03, DE.CM-01, DE.AE-07 and the 12-month retention shortfall at PR.PS-04 in a single project.

CIS:8.12.in: MSP and cloud provider logs are not collected. See DE.CM-06.

CIS:9.1.in: Edge and Chrome kept current via Intune; Outlook is M365 Apps current channel. No unsupported browsers or clients found.

CIS:9.2.in: DNS filtering enforced for all corporate and VPN traffic with category blocking; bypass is prevented at the firewall.

CIS:9.3.in: Sophos web filtering categories are enforced on the corporate network and via the VPN.

CIS:9.4.in: Browser extension installation is not restricted. Users can add extensions from the Chrome Web Store.

CIS:9.5.pn: SPF, DKIM and DMARC required by the email standard.
CIS:9.5.in: SPF and DKIM are correct on both sending domains. DMARC is published at p=quarantine with 100% coverage; the move to p=reject has been open since March.

CIS:9.6.in: Executable, script and macro-bearing file types are blocked at Exchange Online transport rules.

CIS:9.7.in: Defender for Office 365 plus Sophos email protection; Safe Links and Safe Attachments enabled tenant-wide.

CIS:10.2.in: Sophos Central manages signature and engine updates automatically; console shows 100% current.

CIS:10.3.in: Autorun and autoplay disabled by Intune policy across all endpoints.

CIS:10.4.in: Sophos on-access scanning covers removable media.

CIS:10.5.in: Sophos exploit prevention enabled. Windows ASR rules are partially deployed — 6 of the 16 recommended rules are in block mode.

CIS:10.6.in: Sophos Central provides single-console management with alerting; 98% endpoint coverage.

CIS:11.1.pn: Backup standard defines scope, schedule, retention and testing.
CIS:11.1.in: Veeam covers all Tier 1 and Tier 2 systems and M365. The documented quarterly restore test has not run since Q1 2025.

CIS:11.4.in: Immutable Veeam repository plus an offsite copy at Ashbourne; immutability verified during this assessment.

CIS:12.1.in: Firewall firmware is current. Two access switches are past vendor end-of-support and cannot be patched.

CIS:12.3.in: Network devices are managed from the management VLAN with individual accounts; two devices still allow HTTP management.

CIS:12.4.in: HQ diagrams are current. Little Island has not been documented since the 2025 integration.

CIS:12.5.in: Firewalls authenticate to Entra. Switches use local accounts with no central AAA.

CIS:12.6.in: SSH and HTTPS are used for most device management; SNMPv2c is still in use for monitoring.

CIS:12.7.in: Always-on VPN with device compliance; split tunnelling is disabled.

CIS:12.8.in: Administrative work is done from -adm accounts on standard laptops. No dedicated privileged access workstations.

CIS:13.2.in: Sophos EDR provides host-based detection on 98% of endpoints and all servers.

CIS:13.3.in: Sophos XGS IPS is enabled at the perimeter. No internal network detection.

CIS:13.4.in: Firewall rules separate corporate, guest and OT VLANs. Within the corporate VLAN traffic is unrestricted.

CIS:13.5.in: Remote assets must pass Entra device compliance before VPN or M365 access is granted.

CIS:13.6.in: No netflow or traffic flow logging anywhere in the estate.

CIS:13.7.in: Sophos EDR is in block mode on endpoints and servers.

CIS:13.8.in: Perimeter IPS is in prevention mode; no internal IPS.

CIS:13.9.in: No 802.1X or port-level access control. Any device plugged into a wall port at any site reaches the corporate VLAN.

CIS:13.11.in: Alert thresholds are vendor defaults and have never been tuned; alert fatigue in the shared IT mailbox is visible.

CIS:14.2.in: Social engineering is covered in induction, the annual module and monthly simulations. Click rate down from 18% to 6%.

CIS:14.3.in: Authentication and MFA practice is covered in the annual module.

CIS:14.4.in: Data handling training is generic because there is no classification scheme to teach.

CIS:14.5.in: Accidental disclosure and misdirected email are covered in the annual module.

CIS:14.6.pn: Reporting expectations are documented in the incident response plan.
CIS:14.6.in: The Outlook report-phishing button is deployed and used — 214 reports in the period. Staff know how to report; they do not always get feedback.

CIS:14.7.in: Covered in training. There is no simple way for a user to check whether their device is out of date.

CIS:14.8.in: Insecure network use is covered in training and mitigated by always-on VPN.

CIS:16.2.in: No process to accept software vulnerability reports. See ID.RA-08.

CIS:16.4.in: No inventory of third-party components. The Power Platform connectors used by finance are undocumented.

CIS:16.8.in: The ERP has a separate test instance. The Power Platform work is built directly in the production environment.

CIS:16.9.in: The finance staff building Power Apps and Power Automate flows have had no secure development training.

CIS:17.1.pn: The plan names the IT Manager as incident handler and the compliance manager as deputy.
CIS:17.1.in: Both are aware of the role. Neither has formal incident response training and there is no out-of-hours rota.

CIS:17.3.in: Reporting route is documented and the phishing button works well; 214 user reports in the period.

CIS:17.5.pn: Roles are assigned in the plan.
CIS:17.5.in: Assigned but not rehearsed. Two named individuals have left the business.

CIS:17.7.pn: Annual exercises are required by the plan.
CIS:17.7.in: No exercise has ever been run. Top recommendation alongside log centralisation.
CIS:17.7.rec: Run a facilitated tabletop exercise in Q3 covering a ransomware scenario affecting the Ashbourne production systems, with the Operations Director, IT Manager, compliance manager and the MSP present. Use the June 2025 BEC as a warm-up scenario for the first session. Budget half a day and capture the actions in the improvement register.

CIS:18.1.pn: Annual external testing is required by policy.
CIS:18.1.in: Delivered as a one-off purchase rather than a programme; no scope definition or year-on-year comparison.

CIS:18.2.in: External test completed November 2025 by a CREST-accredited provider.

CIS:18.3.pn: Remediation of findings is required within 90 days.
CIS:18.3.in: Six of fourteen findings from the November test remain open past SLA, including one high-severity issue on the customer portal.

CIS:18.4.in: No validation that controls actually work; no purple team or breach simulation activity.

CIS:18.5.in: No internal penetration testing has been performed.
